system.name: QECC-Synth
system.one_liner: an automated compiler that implements quantum error-correction codes on sparse hardware using ancilla-bridge techniques instead of qubit swapping

components.name: Error Syndrome Measurement Circuit
components.role: quantum circuit that entangles a syndrome qubit with data qubits via controlled gates to detect errors

components.name: Code Topology
components.role: connectivity graph required by a QEC code, e.g. degree-4 connectivity for surface codes

components.name: Hardware Topology
components.role: sparse physical qubit connectivity of current quantum hardware, typically degree 2 or 3

components.name: Swapping-Based Solution
components.role: implements ESM circuits by inserting SWAP gates to route distant qubits adjacent for interaction

components.name: Bridging-Based Solution
components.role: connects data qubits via an ancilla bridge instead of swapping, fixing qubit locations and using fewer CNOT gates

content.key_idea: Because QEC code connectivity outpaces sparse hardware connectivity, ancilla-bridge methods can implement error-syndrome circuits with fixed data-qubit locations and fewer gates than swapping-based routing.
content.reading_order: Top row (a-c) frames the mismatch between a code's required connectivity and sparse hardware; bottom row (d-f) contrasts swapping-based routing with the bridging-based solution.

summary: QECC-Synth is an automated compiler for implementing quantum error-correction (QEC) codes on hardware whose qubit connectivity is sparser than a code needs. This six-panel figure sets up that mismatch and previews two solution families. Panel (a) shows a typical error syndrome measurement (ESM) circuit, where a red syndrome qubit is entangled with blue data qubits through yellow controlled-Pauli gates. Panel (b) shows the degree-4 code topology a surface code requires, while panel (c) shows sparse hardware with only degree-2 or degree-3 connectivity, with a bold red 'Gap!' arrow calling out the mismatch. Panels (d) and (e), grouped under 'Swapping-Based Solution', show implementations that insert SWAP gates to route distant qubits together, without and then with fixed data-qubit locations. Panel (f), 'Bridging-Based Solution', shows an ancilla bridge connecting two ancilla qubits, fixing locations while using fewer CNOT gates than swapping. A shared legend (physical/ancilla/data qubit, gate types) applies across all panels.
